problem: "in a state of democracy" rendered "in a democratic state", which suggests a form of government rather than his social condition.
replacement: When the heroes and manners of antiquity are often brought onto the stage, and playwrights faithfully follow the rules of old precedent, that is enough to conclude that the democratic classes have not yet gained the upper hand in the theaters. In the preface to “Britannicus,” Racine very humbly apologizes for having placed Junia among the Vestals, who, according to Aulus Gellius, he says, “admitted no one below six years of age nor above ten.” We may be sure he would neither have accused himself of this offense nor defended himself against criticism if he had been writing for our contemporaries. A fact of this kind shows the state of literature at the time, and it shows the state of society itself as well. A democratic stage does not prove that the nation is in a state of democracy, because, as we have just seen, even in aristocracies democratic tastes may influence the drama. But when the spirit of aristocracy reigns exclusively on the stage, that fact proves beyond refutation that the whole of society is aristocratic. One may boldly infer that the same lettered and learned class that sways the playwrights also commands the people and governs the country.

problem: Conditional "If the effect of democracy is generally to question..." turned into a flat statement.
replacement: When the democratic classes rule the stage, they bring as much license into the way subjects are treated as into the choice of them. The love of the drama is, of all literary tastes, the one most natural to democratic nations, so in these communities the number of authors, of spectators, and of theatrical performances keeps growing. A multitude made up of such different elements, and scattered over so many different places, cannot recognize the same rules or submit to the same laws. No agreement is possible among so many judges, who do not know when they will meet again, and so each one pronounces his own sentence on the play. If the effect of democracy is generally to call into question the authority of all literary rules and conventions, on the stage it abolishes them altogether and puts nothing in their place but the whim of each author and each public.

problem: Term drift: "strictness of manners" (moeurs) left as "manners"; style note requires customs.
replacement: The Americans show very clearly all the different inclinations I have just described when they go to the theater. But it must be admitted that so far very few of them go to the theater at all. Playgoers and plays have increased enormously in the United States over the last forty years, yet the population indulges in this kind of amusement with the greatest reserve. This is due to particular causes that the reader already knows, and a few words will be enough to remind him of them. The Puritans who founded the American republics were not only enemies of amusements; they professed a special horror of the stage. They regarded it as an abominable pastime, and as long as their principles held undivided sway, theatrical performances were completely unknown among them. These opinions of the first fathers of the colony have left very deep marks on the minds of their descendants. The extreme regularity of habits and great strictness of customs seen in the United States have so far put further obstacles in the way of the growth of dramatic art. There are no dramatic subjects in a country that has seen no great political catastrophes and where love always leads by a straight and easy road to marriage. People who spend every weekday making money and Sunday going to church have nothing to attract the muse of Comedy.

problem: Term drift: "the manners and the laws of the nation" (moeurs) rendered "manners"; style note requires customs.
replacement: No part of literature is joined by closer or more numerous ties to the present condition of society than the drama. The drama of one period can never suit the following age if, in the meantime, an important revolution has changed the nation’s customs and laws. The great authors of an earlier age may still be read, but plays written for a different public will not be followed. The playwrights of the past live only in books. The traditional taste of certain individuals, vanity, fashion, or the genius of an actor may sustain or revive the aristocratic drama for a time in a democracy. But it will soon fall away of its own accord, not overthrown but abandoned.

problem: "the old mass" became "the whole mass"; word changed and "old" lost.
replacement: Those who write in democratic ages have another, more dangerous tendency. When the traces of individual action on nations are lost, it often happens that the world keeps moving although the agent that moves it can no longer be found. It becomes extremely difficult to discern and analyze the reasons that act separately on the will of each member of the community and in the end combine to set the old mass in motion. Men are therefore led to believe that this movement is involuntary, and that societies unconsciously obey some superior force ruling over them. But even when the general fact that governs the private will of every individual is supposed to have been discovered on earth, the principle of human free will is not safe. A cause wide enough to affect millions of men at once, and strong enough to bend them all together in the same direction, may well seem irresistible. Having seen that mankind does yield to it, the mind is close to concluding that mankind cannot resist it.

problem: "too eagerly" lost the qualifier "too"; "a trivial one" has an unclear antecedent for "play an insignificant one".
replacement: In aristocratic nations, the men who sit in political assemblies also belong to the aristocracy. Each has a high, settled rank of his own, and his seat in the assembly often matters less to him than his standing in the country. That standing comforts him when he takes no part in debates on public affairs, and it keeps him from trying too eagerly to take a trivial part.
